title: Money map
headline: Money first. Bitcoin second.
summary: What money must do, why savings melt, who really moves your card payments, what the road home costs — and the one idea that makes Bitcoin click. No jargon, no real money.
coachPitch: Start here if money itself feels foggy. Five short stops, then the Bitcoin road opens.

drives.title: Money before Bitcoin
drives.job: Learn what money must do before you touch crypto
drives.outcome: You'll judge any money — cash, bank balance, or bitcoin — by the same five jobs, and you'll know why distance and permission matter.

steps.coachLine: Before roads, the car: money has five jobs. Meet them through a market stall, not a textbook.

tickets.prompt: A street vendor must give change for a large note at a busy stall. Which money does the job?
A family saves for next winter's heating. Which savings still buys heat in six months?
choices: Coins and notes in a tin box

tickets.prompt: A shop prices bread, milk, and soap. What must all three prices share?

steps.ideaBody: Good money is accepted wherever you trade, keeps its value until you spend it, splits into small pieces, travels with you, and prices everything in one shared unit. When any job fails — the shop refuses it, savings melt, or you cannot make change — people quietly switch to a money that works.
steps.objective: After this screen you can name the five jobs and spot which one fails in a story.
steps.whyItMatters: Every crypto pitch claims to be money. The five jobs are your roadworthiness test — run any coin through them before you trust it.
steps.misconception: Money is valuable because the paper or the app says so.
steps.pocketCard: Accepted, holds, splits, travels, counts — five jobs.

quickCheck.question: A village accepts salt for every trade, but last year's salt buys half the grain today. Which money job failed?
quickCheck.explanation: Salt still trades and splits — but savings melt, so the store-of-value job failed.

steps.coachLine: Your aunt's savings jar buys less every year. Nobody stole it — prices moved.

tickets.prompt: Ten years ago a jar of coins bought a winter coat. Today it buys a scarf. What happened?
choices: Someone took coins from the jar
Prices rose while the jar sat still

tickets.prompt: Prices rise every year. Which savings melts fastest?
choices: A savings account paying less than prices rise
A house the family lives in

tickets.prompt: A shopkeeper raises prices every month to keep up. Who feels it first?

steps.ideaBody: Inflation means prices creep up while saved money sits still — so each note buys a little less every year. A salary that never rises and a jar that never grows are both quietly shrinking. People feel it at the market first: the same basket, more notes.
steps.objective: After this screen you can explain inflation as savings melting while prices move.
steps.whyItMatters: Crypto promises 'hard money' that resists the melt. You cannot judge that promise until you have felt the melt in your own basket.
steps.misconception: If I don't spend my savings, they keep their value.
steps.pocketCard: Still money can shrink. Prices move; jars don't.

quickCheck.question: A worker's pay rises 3% but market prices rise 8%. What happened to her?
options: She can buy less than last year
quickCheck.explanation: Her pay grew, but prices grew faster — her basket shrank.

steps.coachLine: Tap a card and no coin travels. Your bank and the shop's bank swap promises — and settle up later.

tickets.prompt: You tap your card for bread. What actually travels in that second?
choices: A coin from your pocket to the till
A promise between banks, settled later
A paper receipt with value inside

tickets.prompt: Your salary 'arrives' but you never touch it. Where is it?
choices: A pile of notes with your name on it
Numbers in the bank's promise ledger
A truck on its way to you

tickets.prompt: Everyone queues to withdraw on the same morning. Why might the bank run out?
choices: It printed too few notes, ever
It lent the promises out and keeps only a fraction

steps.ideaBody: A bank balance is not a box of your notes — it is the bank's promise to pay you back. Card taps and transfers just rewrite who is promised what; real settlement happens behind the curtain, later. Promises are convenient, which is exactly why you must know who made them.
steps.objective: After this screen you can say what moves in a card payment and where your salary really sits.
steps.whyItMatters: Crypto wallets cut the bank out of the promise chain. That is freedom and risk at once — both start from this screen.
steps.misconception: The numbers in my banking app are my cash, sitting somewhere.
steps.pocketCard: Balance = the bank's promise, not a box of cash.

quickCheck.question: The power fails and card machines die, but cash still buys bread. What does that prove?
options: Cash needs no one's permission to work
quickCheck.explanation: Cash settles on the spot with no network and no bank in the middle.

steps.job: Sending money home costs a cut
steps.coachLine: Your brother works two borders away. Every payday he sends money home — and the road takes a toll.

tickets.prompt: He sends 200 home; 184 arrives three days later. Where did the rest go?
choices: The truck burned it as fuel

tickets.prompt: Two agents quote the same 200 transfer. Which costs the family more?
choices: Agent A: 8% fee, arrives in 3 days

tickets.prompt: His mother needs medicine tonight. What matters most?
choices: The lowest fee, whenever it arrives
Money arriving before the pharmacy closes

steps.ideaBody: Moving money across borders means paying the road: a flat fee, a worse exchange rate than the market, and days of waiting. On a 200 transfer the toll can eat a week's groceries. Speed is part of the price — money that arrives after the need has passed arrived too expensive.
steps.objective: After this screen you can price a remittance in fee, rate cut, and waiting time.
steps.whyItMatters: Stablecoins and Bitcoin sell themselves as cheap fast rails. This screen is how you check whether that claim survives contact with your family's pharmacy run.
steps.pocketCard: Every border takes a cut — fee, rate, and waiting.

quickCheck.question: Shop A charges 8% and takes 3 days; shop B charges 2% and arrives tonight. Which family keeps more?
quickCheck.explanation: Lower fee and same-evening arrival — B wins on both parts of the toll.

steps.coachLine: A banknote in your hand asks no permission. Lose it and it's gone — that trade is the whole idea.

tickets.prompt: Which of these spends with nobody's permission?
choices: A gift card with your name on it

tickets.prompt: What makes the banknote different from the balance?
choices: Holding it IS owning it — no account to ask
It is printed on better paper

tickets.prompt: Which of these is most like cash, but works on the internet?
choices: Bitcoin, held in your own wallet

steps.ideaBody: Cash is bearer money: whoever holds it owns it. No account, no password, no permission — but also no refunds and no one to call. A bank balance is the opposite: permission-gated and reversible. Bitcoin was built as bearer money for the internet — the next road teaches you to drive it without crashing.
steps.objective: After this screen you can explain bearer money and why Bitcoin copies cash, not banks.
steps.whyItMatters: Self-custody is the whole exam at the end of the Bitcoin road. This is the first time you meet the trade: freedom in, permission out.
steps.misconception: Digital money always has a company that can reverse it.
steps.pocketCard: Cash: holding is owning. Bitcoin: same idea, online.

quickCheck.question: A friend's wallet app freezes her account. Could that happen with a banknote in her pocket?
options: No — no one can freeze what she holds
quickCheck.explanation: Bearer money has no account to freeze; the trade is that no one can rescue it either.
